title: House committee docs: Commerce approved 580,000 Nvidia AI chips for China under revenue-share plan
subtitle: The Washington Post, citing confidential documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee, says approved buyers included two Chinese tech firms the Pentagon lists as having military ties.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Washington Post reported on Thursday evening — using confidential documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee — that the Commerce Department approved the sale of roughly 580,000 Nvidia AI chips to Chinese buyers under a Trump administration arrangement that takes a share of the revenue. A broader figure in the same disclosures covers both Nvidia and AMD: the Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export or transfer of 879,868 chips across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Friday that no further restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to China were needed. Commerce has defended the approvals as consistent with national security regulations.

The newsworthy detail is not the volume but the customer list. Several approved buyers, according to the committee's documents, appear on the Pentagon's roster of Chinese firms with military ties. The revenue-share structure — an unusual export-control instrument — ties U.S. fiscal interest to the volume of restricted technology leaving the country. That is the opposite of how export controls have historically been priced: the government loses revenue when a sale is blocked, which is why the controls work as a constraint at all. Pairing the license with a cut of the proceeds flips the incentive.

This lands on a week where Nvidia already had problems. Reuters and the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that the SEC is examining Nvidia's accounting, and shares fell nearly 14% on Friday in the worst single-day drop since January 2025. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday's earnings call the company would be 'far more selective' about AI financing deals. Commerce's China license policy was a tailwind for the quarter. If Congress reopens the arrangement — the committee's disclosure is unlikely to be the last — the shape of Nvidia's China revenue in fiscal 2027 could change materially.

A note for learners: export controls are policy instruments, not moral statements. The question to ask about any licensing regime is who sets the price, who collects it, and what the counterfactual sale looks like. A revenue-share model is defensible if the alternative is a leaky unlicensed market; it is harder to defend if the Pentagon has separately flagged the buyer as a military-linked entity. Read the committee documents when they're posted — the names on the license applications are the story.
